units.title: Value-function approximation, linear features and state aggregation
outcomes: Explain why value prediction with shared weights generalizes across states, and what it can no longer represent.
Derive the stochastic-gradient update for the mean-squared value error and state the distribution it assumes.
Predict how state aggregation biases each group's value toward its most visited members.
units.why: Tables cannot cover large or continuous state spaces. Linear approximation is the first generalizer, and its error measure and sampling assumptions decide whether every later deep update is stable.

next.note: Derive semi-gradient TD from the gradient baseline built here.
Replace linear features with a neural action-value function.

study.title: Approximation as supervised examples and the value error
study.locator: Sections 9.1 and 9.2, printed pp. 198-199: the update-as-example view (each update is one pair \(s \to u\)) and the mean-squared value error \(\text{VE}(w) = \sum_s \mu(s)[v_{\pi}(s) - \hat{v}(s, w)]^2\) as Eq. 9.1
study.depth: The authors post the full text free at https://incompleteideas.net. Read the sections there and cite the printed pages above.

study.title: Linear methods, state aggregation and the random-walk demo
study.locator: Sections 9.4 and 9.5, printed pp. 204-210: \(\hat{v}(s, w) = w^\top x(s)\) with gradient \(\nabla \hat{v}(s, w) = x(s)\), Example 9.1 and Figure 9.1 (1000-state random walk, 10 groups of 100 states)

study.title: Fitted value iteration and the curse of dimensionality
study.locator: Lecture 7 (Value-Based RL), Part 3, slides 10 to 14: fitted value iteration, the curse of dimensionality, and fitted Q-iteration as the sample-based bridge

focus: Each tabular update is one supervised example \(s \to u\). Approximation shares the correction across states through the weight vector \(w\).
The error measure weights states by the visitation distribution \(\mu\). An unweighted fit optimizes a different objective than on-policy performance.
In the linear case the gradient is the feature vector itself, so one update moves every state that shares features.
Figure 9.1 shows the consequence: each aggregation group learns one constant, pulled toward its most visited members, with abrupt boundaries between groups.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the linear stochastic-gradient update from \(\text{VE}\) and explain why the leftmost groups in Figure 9.1 sit above the unweighted mean of their members' true values.
traps: Minimizing error on a uniform state sample instead of under \(\mu\). A uniform sweep is already off-policy training, which the next units show can diverge.
Reading more features as strictly better. Under on-policy linear gradients they approach the value error minimum, but under bootstrapping or off-policy data that guarantee lapses.
Blaming the step size for a representation limit. No choice of \(\alpha\) lets a coarse aggregation represent \(v_{\pi}\) inside a group.

selfTest.q: Why does the book call each update \(s \to u\) a training example?
selfTest.a: Each update names an input state and a desired output target, exactly the interface a supervised approximator expects. The reinforcement learning part is how \(u\) is constructed.

selfTest.q: Two states share all features. What happens when one of them is updated?
selfTest.a: Both estimates move together, because the update changes the shared \(w\). The gradient \(\nabla \hat{v} = x(s)\) is identical for both states.

selfTest.q: In Figure 9.1, why do the leftmost group values sit above their members' unweighted mean?
selfTest.a: Right members of those groups carry far larger \(\mu\) weight (state 100 outweighs state 1 more than threefold), so the group constant fits them more closely.

selfTest.q: Does the value error optimum change when visitation changes?
selfTest.a: Yes. \(\text{VE}\) weights by \(\mu\), so a new visitation distribution defines a new objective with generally a new best \(w\).

units.title: Semi-gradient TD, on-policy prediction and value error versus Bellman error
outcomes: Derive the semi-gradient TD(0) update and name the gradient term it drops.
Explain why a Monte Carlo target gives a true gradient while a bootstrapped target does not.
Compute value error and Bellman error on a small example and state which one samples can estimate.
units.why: Every deep value update is a semi-gradient step. If you cannot say which term is dropped, target-network and detachment bugs stay invisible.

next.note: See what breaks when the on-policy assumption made here is removed.
Apply the detach discipline to neural targets and test it.

study.title: Stochastic gradients, gradient Monte Carlo and semi-gradient TD(0)
study.locator: Section 9.3, printed pp. 200-203: Eqs. 9.4 to 9.7, the gradient Monte Carlo box, and the semi-gradient TD(0) box with \(U_t = R_{t+1} + \hat{v}(S_{t+1}, w)\). The key sentence is that these methods account for the effect on the estimate but ignore the effect on the target.

study.title: Why the Bellman error is not learnable
study.locator: Section 11.6, printed pp. 274-275: the learnability argument, the two-MRP example with identical features but different Bellman error, and the double-sampling requirement

focus: A true gradient needs the target independent of \(w\). Bootstrapped targets depend on \(w_t\), so the step from Eq. 9.4 to Eq. 9.5 is invalid and only part of the gradient is used.

Gradient Monte Carlo converges to a local value error optimum under standard step-size conditions. Semi-gradient TD(0) converges in the linear on-policy case, but that does not make it true gradient descent.
The value error needs the true \(v_{\pi}\). The Bellman error squares an expectation, so estimating it needs two independent next-state samples; one sample used twice biases it.
On-policy prediction means states arrive under the target policy's \(\mu\). Change the sampling distribution and the fixed point moves.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute one linear semi-gradient TD(0) step with features \(x = [1, 0]\), weights \(w = [0.5, 0.5]\), reward \(r = 1\), a terminal next state, \(\gamma = 0.9\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\): show \(\delta = 0.5\) and the new \(w = [0.55, 0.5]\). Then state which gradient term was ignored.
traps: Calling TD(0) a gradient method on the value error. The target-dependence term is dropped in every update.
Reading zero TD error as zero value error. Zero TD error marks the TD fixed point, which generally differs from the value error minimum.
Trusting a small single-sample Bellman residual. Without double sampling the estimate is biased, and minimizing it can prefer the wrong function.

selfTest.q: Which step of the SGD derivation fails for bootstrapped targets?
selfTest.a: From Eq. 9.4 to Eq. 9.5. Moving the gradient inside the square requires the target to be independent of \(w\), but bootstrapped targets depend on \(w_t\).

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, what changes if the transition is non-terminal with \(\hat{v}(s') = 2.0\)?
Why does the Bellman error need two independent next-state samples?
selfTest.a: Its square contains an expectation inside the square. Reusing one sample for both factors correlates them and biases the estimate.

selfTest.q: Linear on-policy TD(0) converges, yet the book still calls it semi-gradient. Why?
selfTest.a: Convergence in that restricted case does not make it true gradient descent. The term from the target's dependence on \(w\) is still dropped.

units.title: Off-policy bootstrapping, the deadly triad and Baird's counterexample
outcomes: Work through Baird's counterexample and name the update direction that causes instability.
State the three triad elements and why any two alone avoid this failure.
Run a controlled divergence demonstration with a stable comparator and keep the divergent trajectory.
units.why: This is the cheapest divergence in reinforcement learning: zero reward with an exactly representable truth. Replay buffers and target networks exist because of this failure.

next.note: Build the replay and target machinery that stabilizes what diverges here.
Control how fast bootstrapped labels may move.

study.title: Off-policy divergence and Baird's counterexample
study.locator: Section 11.2, printed pp. 260-263: the two-state \(w\) versus \(2w\) warm-up (unstable whenever \(\gamma > 0.5\)), the seven-state Baird setup, Figure 11.1, and Figure 11.2 (semi-gradient TD on the left, semi-gradient DP on the right, both diverging from initial weights \((1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 10, 1)\) with \(\alpha = 0.01\))

study.title: The deadly triad
study.locator: Section 11.3, printed pp. 264-265: the three-element definition (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy training), why uniform dynamic-programming sweeps count as off-policy, and Exercise 11.3 (semi-gradient Q-learning on Baird's counterexample)

focus: In the warm-up, each visit multiplies \(w\) by \(1 + \alpha(2\gamma - 1)\). Instability needs only \(\gamma > 0.5\), for every positive step size.

Baird's truth is all zeros and is exactly representable with linearly independent features, yet off-policy semi-gradient TD(0) diverges for any \(\alpha > 0\). Representability never implied stability.
Uniform dynamic-programming sweeps are off-policy here: uniform updates differ from the target policy's concentration on the seventh state.
The on-policy distribution keeps the promise of future reward payable. Off-policy lets a promise be made, then forgotten after an action the target policy never takes.
units.reproduce: From the book's initial weights with \(\alpha = 0.01\), \(\gamma = 0.99\), uniform starts and behavior that takes the dashed action with probability \(6/7\), run 1000 off-policy semi-gradient TD(0) steps on CPU and show the weight norm grows past 700 from 10.3 (a run gives \(w_1 \approx 213.7\) and \(w_8 \approx 544.5\)). Then run the on-policy twin and show it stays bounded.
traps: Blaming reward or representation. Baird has zero reward everywhere and an exact, linearly independent representation.
Shrinking the step size as a fix. A smaller \(\alpha\) only slows the blowup because the per-update factor still exceeds 1.
Trusting expected (dynamic-programming) updates as safe. Figure 11.2 shows semi-gradient DP diverging too; only the on-policy distribution change stabilizes.

selfTest.q: In the warm-up with \(\gamma = 0.9\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\), what is the per-update multiplier?
selfTest.a: \(1 + 0.1 \times (2 \times 0.9 - 1) = 1.08\). Each visit grows \(w\) by about 8 percent.

selfTest.q: Why is uniform dynamic programming off-policy training in this example?
selfTest.a: Its update distribution is uniform over states while the target policy concentrates on the seventh state. The triad's off-policy leg is about distributions, not about sampling noise.

selfTest.q: The true values are all zero and exactly representable. Why is divergence not a contradiction?
selfTest.a: Representability does not imply stability. Under the wrong update distribution the semi-gradient direction at \(w = 0\) points away from it.

selfTest.q: Which single triad leg would you remove to keep bootstrapping and approximation?
selfTest.a: Train on-policy, so ratios are 1 and visitation matches the target policy. Removing bootstrapping (Monte Carlo targets) is the alternative, at steep sample cost.

study.title: Deep Q-learning with experience replay
study.locator: Algorithm 1 and Section 4 in arXiv:1312.5602v1 (the three replay advantages: data efficiency, decorrelation, behavior averaging). Read Section 5 as reported Atari protocol, not as reproduction targets. Note this version has no target network: targets use the previous iterate.

focus: One forward pass outputs every discrete-action value, and `argmax` selects among them. Continuous actions need a different method entirely.
The loss compares the prediction selected by `gather` against a target built under `torch.no_grad()` from the frozen network. Gradients must touch only the prediction.
The workshop paper fixes targets with the previous iterate, not a periodic copy. The frozen-network copy used in code is the later stabilization of the same idea.
Training explores while evaluation acts greedy. A test score measured with exploration mixes luck with learning.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, trace one update on a batch of two with \(\gamma = 0.99\): a non-terminal transition with \(r = 1\), max next-Q 3.0 and current Q 2.0, plus a terminal transition with \(r = -1\) and current Q 0.5. Show targets 3.97 and -1.0 with mean squared error 3.06545.
traps: Copying the first page's target verbatim. It omits the terminal mask, so terminal transitions bootstrap phantom future value.
Reusing the online network for targets. That reintroduces the moving-target loop the frozen network exists to slow.
Judging training by episode return alone. The paper's Section 5.1 shows return is noisy under shifting visitation, so track average predicted Q on a fixed state set too.

selfTest.q: Why output all action values at once instead of one value per forward pass?
selfTest.a: One pass plus `argmax` scores every discrete action. Per-action passes would multiply inference cost by the action count.

selfTest.q: What does `gather` do in the update?
selfTest.a: It selects, for each batch row, the Q-value of the action actually taken, so the loss touches only visited state-action pairs.

selfTest.q: The workshop target uses the previous iterate. What breaks if targets use freshly updated weights every step?
selfTest.a: Prediction and target share parameters, so each update moves the label it just chased. The loss has no fixed label inside the step.

selfTest.q: A CartPole agent scores 500 in testing but 200 in training. Is it broken?
selfTest.a: No. Training mixes random exploratory actions while the test is greedy. Compare greedy with greedy.

units.title: Transition immutability, replay aliasing, replay age and policy drift

Explain replay age and policy drift: old transitions come from worse policies.
Detect an autoreset artifact and a stale-data slowdown in your own buffer.
units.why: A replay buffer is a dataset with an expiration date. One stored fake transition or a diet of ancient data silently changes the objective.

study.locator: Experience Replay: the five-tuple table, the capacity range (\(10^4\) to \(10^6\)), and the stale-experience warning for oversized buffers

study.title: Termination, truncation and the autoreset step
study.locator: Termination, Truncation, Importance in learning code, and Solution. Under the default next-step autoreset in Gymnasium 1.x, the step after an episode ends returns reward 0 with both flags false: that output is not a transition and must not be stored.

study.title: What version-skewed storage code looks like
study.locator: The `dqn.py` storage lines that read `final_observation` and `final_info`. They are correct for `gymnasium==0.29.1` and raise `KeyError` at truncation on Gymnasium 1.x, where those keys no longer exist

focus: A transition is an immutable record. Overwriting a stored next-state (for example with a reset observation) rewrites history, and every reuse of that row learns from a fabricated pair.
Termination cuts bootstrapping through \((1 - d) = 0\). Truncation keeps it. Storing both the same way undervalues every state near a time limit.
Capacity sets the age distribution, not just memory. Too small loses diversity; too large preserves data from long-obsolete policies that drags current values.
CleanRL `dqn.py` expects same-step info keys, so on Gymnasium 1.x it logs no episode returns and crashes at truncation. Pin `gymnasium==0.29.1` or patch those lines.
units.reproduce: On Gymnasium 1.4.0 with `CartPole-v1`, `max_episode_steps=5` and `seed=0`, show steps 0 to 4 returning reward 1.0 with truncation at step 4, and the next step returning reward 0.0 with both flags false. State which of the six outputs is storable: only the first five.
traps: Treating the autoreset output as a transition. Reward 0 with cleared flags is the reset handshake, not experience.
Quoting capacity without interaction rate. A million stored transitions from a random early policy is mostly drift, not diversity.
Assuming more replay is always more stable. Stale data from a far worse policy can anchor values away from the current policy's truth.

selfTest.q: The vector env returns reward 0.0 with both flags false right after an episode ended. Store it?
selfTest.a: No. That is the next-step autoreset output: a fresh observation with a dummy reward, not a transition the policy experienced.

selfTest.q: A stored transition's next-state is later overwritten with the reset observation. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Its TD target bootstraps from an unrelated state. Every sample reusing that row learns from a fabricated pair.

selfTest.q: The buffer holds a million transitions but the policy improved sharply 50k steps ago. Concern?
selfTest.a: Most samples come from the old policy. Gradients optimize a stale distribution and can slow or drag the new policy's values.

selfTest.q: CleanRL `dqn.py` prints `SPS` but no episodic returns on your install. First check?
selfTest.a: The Gymnasium version. On 1.x the `final_info` branch never fires, so confirm the version before touching the algorithm.

units.why: The target network sets how fast the label may move. Too fresh chases its tail, too stale teaches yesterday's values, and too many updates per sample overfits the buffer.

study.locator: Lecture 8, Part 2, slides 9 to 13: data collection, target updates and regression as three processes, the update-to-data ratio, and the overfitting warning for too-high values

study.title: One concrete operating point
study.locator: The `dqn.py` hyperparameters and Implementation details: `target_network_frequency=500` with `tau=1.0`, which in Polyak form is a full hard copy

study.title: Freezing targets as the DQN fix
study.locator: Lecture 06 (Q-learning), slides 16 and 17: the lecture plan and freezing target parameters with periodic updates (the DQN algorithm)

focus: A hard copy sets \(\theta^{-} \leftarrow \theta\) every \(N\) steps and holds labels fixed between copies. Polyak sets \(\theta^{-} \leftarrow \tau\theta + (1 - \tau)\theta^{-}\) every update. With \(\tau = 1.0\) the Polyak form is a hard copy.
The lecture's 10,000-step period and CleanRL's 500-step default are different operating points, not conflicting truths. The right lag depends on update frequency and task speed.
Replay ratio (update-to-data ratio) is gradient updates per environment step. Raising it learns faster per sample but costs compute and can overfit buffer noise.
Fitted Q-iteration is the extreme of many updates per collection round; online Q-learning is the other. DQN sits between them.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute one Polyak step with \(\tau = 0.005\), \(\theta = 2.0\) and \(\theta^{-} = 1.0\): show 1.005. Then state what \(\tau = 1.0\) does to the same formula.
traps: Reading small \(\tau\) as slow learning. It means slow label movement; per-sample learning can still be fast through the update ratio.
Copying targets every step for freshness. That deletes the stabilization the target network exists for.
Comparing two update ratios by episode count. Episodes hide the compute and data difference; match environment steps and report wall time.

selfTest.q: CleanRL sets `tau=1.0` yet calls it a Polyak update. Contradiction?
selfTest.a: No. The update has Polyak form, and with \(\tau = 1.0\) it copies fully, which equals a hard update every `target_network_frequency` steps.

selfTest.q: You raise the update ratio from 1 to 8 with episodes matched and declare victory. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: Environment steps and compute differ eightfold. Match the interaction budget and report wall time before claiming efficiency.

selfTest.q: Values look stale with targets copied every 10,000 steps. First knob?
selfTest.a: Shorten the target period while watching TD-error variance. Fresher labels track faster but move more.

selfTest.q: Why does the lecture warn that too high an update ratio overfits?
selfTest.a: Repeated updates on the same buffer rows fit sampling noise and a stale distribution instead of the task.

study.title: The update method line by line
study.locator: The `update` method: `gather` for the taken action, `torch.no_grad()` around the masked target, mean squared error, and `clip_grad_norm_` with `max_norm=10`

study.title: The mask authority
study.locator: Importance in learning code and Solution: bootstrap on truncation, cut on termination, with target `rew + gamma * (1 - terminated) * value_next`

study.title: The single-file update to test against
study.locator: The ALGO LOGIC block: `with torch.no_grad()` target with `.max(dim=1)`, `.gather(1, ...)` prediction, mean squared error, and the Polyak-form target copy

focus: The mask multiplies by \((1 - d)\) with \(d\) as terminated only. Truncation keeps the bootstrap; the tutorial's Solution section is explicit.
Detachment makes targets constants: gradients flow only through \(Q(s, a; \theta)\). Without it, backpropagation also pulls the label.
`gather` on stored actions selects visited pairs; `max` over next-state values selects the bootstrap action. Swapping them trains the wrong pairing.
Frozen batches with frozen nets give bit-reproducible targets. Any mismatch after a code change is a bug, not noise.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the two-transition hand targets from the replay unit (3.97 and -1.0, mean squared error 3.06545) and write the frozen-batch assertion your update must satisfy to four decimals.
traps: Masking with terminated-or-truncated. Time-limit states lose their bootstrap and their values collapse near the cutoff.
Detaching the max index but not the value, or the reverse. The whole target expression must be constant, not half of it.
Testing with live sampling. Randomness hides systematic target bugs; freeze the batch first, then test.

selfTest.q: Your mask uses terminated-or-truncated. Which states lose value and why?
selfTest.a: States near the time limit. Their targets drop the bootstrap term, so values ignore everything past the cutoff although the task continues.

selfTest.q: Loss falls on live samples but the policy stays random. What is the next test?
selfTest.a: Freeze one batch with hand targets. A falling live loss can come from shrinking target scale while the policy stays poor.

selfTest.q: What exactly changes when `torch.no_grad()` is removed from the target?
selfTest.a: The target joins the computation graph, so `backward` also moves target-net outputs to minimize the loss. The update chases its own label.

selfTest.q: The gather uses `argmax` over current Q instead of stored actions. What does the loss train?
selfTest.a: Values of greedy actions rather than visited pairs. Off-policy data is misread as on-policy greedy data.

study.locator: Section 5 in arXiv:1312.5602v1 (training-only clipping of positive rewards to +1 and negative rewards to -1, with the stated cost that the agent cannot tell magnitudes apart) and Section 5.1 (noisy episode return versus smooth average predicted Q on a fixed random-policy state set)

study.title: Practical stabilization tips
study.locator: Lecture 8, slides 21 and 22: test on easy tasks first, large replay buffers, \(\epsilon\) schedules, gradient clipping or Huber loss, Double Q-learning, and multiple seeds

study.title: Loss, clipping and evaluation in code
study.locator: The `update` loss lines (mean squared error with `clip_grad_norm_` at `max_norm=10`) and the greedy evaluation with `epsilon=0.0`. Note the file stores terminated only, which is the correct mask.

focus: Clipping maps every positive reward to +1, so one learning rate works across games. The price is explicit in the paper: magnitudes above 1 become indistinguishable.

The paper's remedy for noisy evaluation is a fixed state set from a random policy with average predicted max-Q. Smooth Q with flat return means values learn while behavior still explores, not the reverse.
Early runs can look random for a while. Impatient restarts destroy the multi-seed evidence the comparison needs.
CartPole needs no clipping or scaling. The diagnostic habit (Q mean, TD loss, gradient norm) transfers to tasks that do.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map the rewards 5.0, -0.2 and 0.0 through the paper's training clip, and state which two signals the fixed-state average-Q plot separates. Answers: 1, -1 and 0; it separates value-estimate progress from behavior and visitation noise.
traps: Calling clipping a pure rescale. It requantizes: a bonus of 10 and a bonus of 1000 train identically, which can change the optimal policy.
Reading raw episode return as the learning signal during heavy exploration. The policy visits new states as it learns, so return confounds behavior with values.
Copying Atari preprocessing onto CartPole and expecting paper curves. Scale choices are task-specific, not portable defaults.

selfTest.q: A game pays 10 or 1000 for two bonuses. What does the clipped agent learn to prefer?
selfTest.a: Neither systematically. Both train as +1, so the agent cannot learn the magnitude difference. That is the stated cost of clipping.

selfTest.q: Average Q rises smoothly while episode return thrashes. Verdict?
selfTest.a: Keep training. Values improve on the fixed set while behavior still explores new visitation. The paper's Section 5.1 names exactly this split.

selfTest.q: Gradients explode after removing gradient clipping. What do you check before restoring it?
selfTest.a: Target and reward scale first. A huge TD error from a wrong mask or unclipped magnitudes is the cause; clipping would only hide it.

selfTest.q: Two identical-code CartPole runs differ by 200 return. Next step?
selfTest.a: Run more seeds before changing code. Runs are very inconsistent between seeds, so one pair proves nothing.

units.title: Maximization bias, double estimators and dueling networks
outcomes: Derive the double-estimator split and show the bias it removes on a noisy example.
Implement double DQN as a two-line target change evaluated on identical samples.
Write the dueling aggregation and explain what the mean subtraction identifies.
units.why: The max operator prefers noise. Double estimation removes the preference without new data, and dueling separates state goodness from action choice.

next.note: Freeze the estimator comparison in a full checkpoint.
Reuse the detach and target discipline for learned value baselines.

study.title: Overestimation and the double target
study.locator: Section 2 (the max-bias argument) and the Double DQN target equation in arXiv:1509.06461v3: select with online weights, evaluate with target weights. Read the Atari table as the paper's reported numbers.

study.title: Overestimation plots and double Q in lecture form
study.locator: Lecture 8, Part 3, slides 14 to 20: Q-accuracy plots, overestimation, Double Q-learning in practice, and generalized double Q-learning

study.title: Dueling aggregation and identifiability
study.locator: Section 3 in arXiv:1511.06581v3, Equations 7 to 9: the unidentifiable naive sum, the max-subtracted form, and the mean-subtracted form used in practice. Section 4.1 (corridor policy evaluation) shows where the structure helps.

study.title: Both improvements in code
study.locator: Double DQN (the selection versus evaluation split with its PyTorch snippet) and Dueling DQN (value and advantage streams with mean recombination)

focus: The max over noisy estimates is biased upward: \(\mathbb{E}[\max_a \hat{Q}] \ge \max_a \mathbb{E}[\hat{Q}]\). Double DQN selects with online weights and evaluates with target weights.
The code change is two lines (`argmax` on one net, `gather` on the other). Compare against vanilla on identical samples and budgets, or the comparison is void.

The naive sum \(Q = V + A\) is unidentifiable: a constant shift cancels. Max-subtraction pins the best action's advantage at zero; the mean form used in practice stabilizes by moving only with the mean.
Dueling helps where state value dominates action differences. It does not fix overestimation; that is the double split's job.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the double target for online next-values \([1.0, 2.5, 2.0]\), target next-values \([0.0, 1.0, 5.0]\), \(r = 0\), \(\gamma = 0.99\) and no termination: show 0.99 against a vanilla 4.95. Then show two uniform noise draws over \([-0.5, 0.5]\) give \(\mathbb{E}[\max] = 0.25\) above the true zero.
traps: Selecting with the target net and evaluating with the online net. The backwards split reintroduces bias through the noisier leg.
Reading the dueling value stream as the state value under naive-sum semantics. Only the max form makes \(V\) estimate the best action's value; the mean form is off by a constant.
Crediting double for a win on different samples, seeds or tuning. The paper's same-protocol discipline is load-bearing.

selfTest.q: Online ranks action 2 best while the target values action 3 highest. Which number enters the double target?
selfTest.a: The target net's value for action 2. Selection is online and evaluation is target; the highest target value is never touched.

selfTest.q: Why does the bias grow with more actions?
selfTest.a: More draws raise the expected maximum of the noise. The max has more chances to catch an upward error.

selfTest.q: Add 5 to \(V\) and subtract 5 from every \(A\) under the naive sum. What changes?
selfTest.a: Nothing in \(Q\): the shift cancels, which is the unidentifiability. Under the mean form the same shift moves \(Q\) by 5, so the decomposition is pinned.

selfTest.q: Dueling speeds up LunarLander hovering but overestimation persists. Expected?
selfTest.a: Yes. Dueling restructures credit between state and actions; it does not remove max bias. Add the double split for that.

units.title: Checkpointing model, optimizer, replay and RNG, and separating evaluation exploration
outcomes: List the full resume state: model, optimizer, replay, RNG streams and counters.
Separate training exploration from evaluation and hold the evaluation protocol fixed.
Interrupt and resume a run with identical continuation.
units.why: A checkpoint without replay or RNG state resumes a different experiment. Evaluation that still explores measures luck, not learning.

next.note: Extend the fixed evaluation protocol to multi-seed uncertainty.
Extend checkpoint identity to rollout and policy versions.

study.title: Training versus inference modes
study.locator: The Learning versus Inference comparison: exploratory collection with replay and target updates during training, pure greedy action with no updates during evaluation

study.title: What a model-only checkpoint omits
study.locator: The save lines (`torch.save` of the Q-network state dict only). Fine for publishing a policy, but with no optimizer, replay or RNG state it cannot resume training identically.

study.title: Seeding and deterministic evaluation
study.locator: The environment seeding contract (`reset` with a seed) plus the autoreset note. Fix environment, policy, seed set and episode count for evaluation; keep training-time randomness out.

focus: Resume state means parameters, optimizer state, replay contents and cursor, every RNG stream, and the step and exploration-schedule positions. Missing one piece continues a different trajectory.
Both reference scripts persist the model only. That publishes a policy but does not resume an experiment.
Evaluation fixes the policy to greedy, the seed set, the episode count and the environment version. Training \(\epsilon\) and wrapper changes must not leak in.
The checkpoint must record the same identity fields the trajectory schema demands: environment, policy, seed and code versions.
units.reproduce: Write the checkpoint dictionary keys for a CartPole DQN (parameters, optimizer, replay contents and cursor, Python, NumPy and Torch RNG states, global step, \(\epsilon\) position), interrupt a run, and show the resumed loss trajectory matches the uninterrupted one.
traps: Equating a saved model with reproducibility. Weights without optimizer, replay and RNG state restart the trajectory elsewhere.
Evaluating with training \(\epsilon\) for fairness. Shared noise still inflates variance and can flip close rankings; report greedy scores and training curves separately.
Re-seeding evaluation environments per checkpoint. Sampling differences then masquerade as policy differences.

selfTest.q: A resumed run from a model-only checkpoint diverges from the original curve. Bug?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. Optimizer momentum, replay contents and RNG streams restarted fresh, so the trajectory differs by construction. Persist full state or record the difference.

selfTest.q: Evaluation uses \(\epsilon = 0.05\) like training. What is the cost?
selfTest.a: Random actions contaminate the score. Small-sample comparisons then measure exploration luck instead of policy quality.

selfTest.q: Which RNG streams must a CPU CartPole checkpoint capture?
selfTest.a: Python `random`, NumPy and Torch generators, plus the environment seed: action sampling, buffer sampling, initialization and environment stochasticity each draw from one.

selfTest.q: The environment version bumps mid-project. Keep the old checkpoints?
selfTest.a: Keep them but re-evaluate under the new version with fixed seeds. Never mix returns across versions in one curve.
